title: Procedural coastline + city map generator (vector, seeded, campaign-mutable)
summary: Replace the AI-generated satellite battle map with a seeded, vector, procedurally-generated map of the city and its coast at Cities-Skylines density — terrain by real erosion simulation, coastline by flooding the resulting valleys, city by tensor-field streets down to every alley and roadside shrine — architected so the map can be built on and blown up across the whole 8-level campaign, and so its elevation model drives a real line-of-sight system for Frames.
description:
Ingram's framing, verbatim: "I have a satellite image of the coast that I'm using as a battle map but it's very ugly." Two questions asked — (1) how hard is a really realistic, highly detailed Japanese-style coastline generated procedurally, including an ocean floor, half-remembering a research paper about generating terrain by "only building nearby new chunks based on a comparison of local areas"; (2) could we build a procedural city map generator where "the roads would just be points, they wouldn't have to actually work," but detailed enough to fill the map with buildings. Stated goal: a map updated as the campaign goes along, detailed enough that players can see individual houses as rough rectangles and read road names and ferry terminals, and when an explosion happens the map is updated with a chunk carved out of it. Explicit instruction: "you aren't allowed to think of less than the best."

TWO REFRAMES accepted in the same conversation, both load-bearing:

(a) These are NOT two projects. Terrain is the planning substrate the city is derived from, not scenery behind it. The pipeline is elevation → water → coastline → buildable land → roads → blocks → parcels → buildings → names, each stage consuming the last. This is what makes a town look SITED rather than sprinkled.

(b) Don't generate a picture; generate a world model that renders to a picture. Required by the 'carve a chunk out when an explosion happens' goal, and an architectural decision that has to be made on day one rather than retrofitted.

ONE PUSHBACK, accepted: roads should be a real planar graph, not disconnected points (Ingram's original framing was that "the roads would just be points, they wouldn't have to actually work"). Barely harder, and it is what enables block extraction, buildings that all touch a street, address generation, routing, and making a severed bridge mean something.

CRITIQUE OF THE CURRENT ASSET (tools/battle-simulator/assets/battle-map.jpg): mush under zoom — roads dissolve into noise, buildings are smears, no readable text, no semantic layer — and the palette reads arid Mediterranean/Anatolian (tan, sparse, dry riverbed) rather than the wet, dark-green, densely terraced Japan the setting calls for. It also cannot be updated, which is the disqualifying problem.

--- PROBLEM 1: TERRAIN ---

The half-remembered paper is patch-based / local-neighbourhood synthesis. Lineage: Efros & Freeman, Image Quilting (2001) → Zhou, Sun, Turk & Rehg, 'Terrain Synthesis from Digital Elevation Models' (2007), which is literally 'build new chunks by comparing local areas against real terrain' → Merrell, Model Synthesis (2007) and Gumin, WaveFunctionCollapse (2016), whose rule is that every NxN local neighbourhood in the output must appear somewhere in the input.

Key technical judgment: WFC/patch synthesis is the WRONG tool for terrain structure and the RIGHT tool for terrain texture. It is locally-constrained by definition and therefore cannot guarantee long-range coherence — it cannot promise a river reaches the sea, because that is a global property. Erosion simulation is the opposite: globally coherent by construction. So structure comes from physics, character comes from patch synthesis.

Layer A — structure from physics. No Perlin/fBm as a base (noise gives cloud-blobs; real land has drainage structure, and the eye knows). Cordonnier et al., 'Large Scale Terrain Generation from Tectonic Uplift and Fluvial Erosion' (Eurographics 2016): an uplift field plus the iterated stream power equation dh/dt = U - K*A^m*S^n over upstream drainage area A and slope S. Braun & Willett (2013) give an implicit O(n) scheme, unconditionally stable — seconds in JS at map resolution. For Japan: high uplift + high precipitation, the parameter regime that produces short, steep, aggressive rivers and densely dissected young mountains.

Layer B — the coastline trick. Do not generate a coastline; generate terrain and FLOOD it. A ria coast (リアス式海岸 — Sanriku, Shima, Wakasa Bay) is literally a drowned river-valley network. Erode to a dissected landscape, pick a sea level, take the contour: deeply-indented branching coast, sheltered natural harbours at every valley mouth, headlands between them, offshore islands from isolated hilltops — all causally correct rather than mimicked. Adding a deposition term (Davy & Lague 2009) yields alluvial fans and flat valley floors at river mouths, which IS the pocket of buildable land where a Japanese coastal town goes. The city site generates itself. Note this also reproduces the reference art's channel with cliff-terraced old town on one side and industrial flats on the other: a drowned valley with an asymmetric cross-section, steep cut-bank vs depositional terrace.

Layer C — ocean floor. The same eroded surface continued below sea level (submarine canyons at river mouths — real and dramatic in Japan), plus a wave-cut shore platform, plus sediment infill modelled as diffusion weighted by wave exposure (bays silt to mud flats, exposed headlands stay rocky), plus a shelf break dropping fast to deep water — authentic here, since the Nankai Trough and Japan Trench run close inshore. Bathymetry to be quantized into gameplay-legible depth bands (wadeable / swimmable / boat-navigable / Frame-submerged), on the principle that the map is a game object and every layer should emit a beauty pass AND a rules pass.

Layer D — amplification (optional polish). Patch-synthesis transfer of real Japanese DEM character (hillslope roughness, terracing, gully texture) onto the physics-derived structure. Layers A-C are ~90% of the realism at map zoom; only reach for D if hillsides look too smooth.

--- PROBLEM 2: THE CITY ---

Streets via tensor fields, not L-systems. Parish & Müller (2001) is the classic (it became CityEngine) but the better fit is Chen, Esch, Wonka, Müller & Zhang, 'Interactive Procedural Street Modeling' (2008): define a tensor field over the terrain, trace streamlines, major roads on one eigenvector and minor roads on the perpendicular. Exactly right for Japan because Japanese urban form is famously NOT a grid — organic accretion following topography and old field boundaries. Tensor fields blend regimes within one town: contour-following on the terraced hillside (roads that traverse rather than climb — the signature look), shore-parallel at the waterfront, radial around shrine and station, and a small orthogonal grid in the post-war reclaimed harbour district sitting at an obvious angle to everything else — a period-authentic tell of 1950s reconstruction.

Hierarchy: arterial → collector → local → roji (路地, the tiny alleys, the single most Japanese thing on the map), generated the way they really formed: after blocks exist, punch a dead-end alley into any block too deep for every parcel to reach a street.

Blocks → parcels → buildings. Planar-graph face extraction for blocks; recursive oriented-bounding-box splitting perpendicular to street frontage for parcels (Vanegas et al., 'Procedural Generation of Parcels in Urban Modeling', 2012), with jitter and occasional refusal-to-split for irregularity. Japanese calibration: small lots (~100-165 m², 30-50 tsubo), long-thin 'eel bed' (鰻の寝床) frontages in old merchant districts, near-zero setbacks. Footprint = parcel minus setback, notched into L-shapes and courtyards. Roofs via STRAIGHT SKELETON, which yields ridge and hip lines for free — precisely what a Japanese town looks like from above, a dense field of tiled roof polygons with visible ridgelines (irimoya / kirizuma / yosemune).

Land use before buildings: a zoning field DERIVED from terrain plus accessibility (distance-to-water, distance-to-arterial) rather than painted — harbour/industry on the flats, commerce along the arterial and near the station, residential climbing the hillside, terraced agriculture at the fringe, shrine on a hill spur with a stepped approach.

Naming, which is what makes it readable and is nearly free: Japanese toponymy is highly compositional (〜町 chō, 〜丁目 chōme, 〜通り dōri, 〜坂 saka for a hill road, 〜橋 bashi, 〜港 kō, 〜浜 hama, 〜崎 saki, 〜湾 wan). Derive names FROM the terrain generated in Problem 1 — the road climbing the bluff becomes a 〜坂, the shore road becomes 浜通り, the bay takes its name from the sheltering headland. That derivation is the whole difference between 'authored' and 'random'. Structural bonus: Japanese addresses are block-based, not street-based (chōme-banchi-gō), so the block extraction step IS the addressing system.

--- THE UPDATABILITY ARCHITECTURE (the part that matters most) ---

Directly serves campaign-arc.md's stated commitment that 'the city takes real, visible scars' — a destructible map is the throughline made literal, not a gimmick.

- Deterministic hierarchical seeding: seed → terrain → roads → blocks → parcels → buildings, so any subtree regenerates identically. IDs derive from hierarchy position, never a counter (the same trick the Foundry module already uses).
- Damage is an APPEND-ONLY EVENT LOG, never a destructive edit: {type: 'crater', center, radiusM, at: 'day-14', cause: 'claimant-sweep'}. Render = base scene + replayed events. Yields undo, before/after, and a time-lapse of the city degrading across all 8 levels — potentially the most affecting handout in the campaign given the 'enduring, not restoring' theme.
- GM hand-edits are events too ({type: 'override', id: 'bldg-...'}), so regeneration never clobbers authored content.
- SVG as the canonical render: text stays real text (labels along textPath), zoom is free, and carving a crater is a geometric boolean rather than painting over pixels.
- Then bake for Foundry: SVG → raster background tiles, PLUS building footprints → wall segments for line-of-sight. Auto-generated walls for an entire town is independently valuable and infeasible by hand.
- The named statblocked assets civilian-protection-combat-layer needs become a query against the semantic layer (ferry terminal, gasworks, causeway, a named tenement block), not a separate hand-authored list.

--- HONEST RISKS ---

- The real cost is the art-direction tuning loop, not any algorithm. Every technique above is documented and tractable; making the output look specifically 1950s Japanese rather than generic-Europe-with-different-roofs is a hundred small parameter judgments. Argues for a fast preview/inspect UI early (the battle-sim replay scrubber is the existing pattern).
- Map label placement is classically annoying (curved text, collision avoidance, priority). Solvable with greedy placement + textPath; budget real time.
- Named alternative: the most realistic Japanese coastline is a real one. Japan's GSI publishes 5m DEM; GEBCO/JTOPO cover bathymetry. Warping an anonymized real ria coast would give unimpeachable realism for a fraction of the work. Judged NOT the right call — authorial control and campaign-long mutability don't survive a fixed real-world extract — but real DEM is an excellent exemplar for Layer D and the honest fallback if Layer A tuning stalls.
- Testing fits unusually well (per the project's every-feature-ships-with-a-test rule): determinism (same seed → identical output) plus invariants (every parcel touches a road, no building below sea level, flow graph acyclic, road network connected, damage events idempotent). Property tests, not golden files.

--- STAGED PLAN ---

Ordered so each stage is independently useful even if the next never happens:
1. Erosion + flood → coastline and bathymetry, rendered as hillshaded SVG. Alone this replaces the current map with something better.
2. Tensor-field roads + block extraction + naming.
3. Parcels, footprints, roofs.
4. Damage event log + Foundry bake.

Ingram's response to the above: 'write up the idea entry, then show me a coastline' — i.e. proceed, starting at stage 1.

=== SCOPE EXPANSION, 2026-08-23 (second conversation) ===

Ingram's response to stage 1: 'a really promising start', and then a substantially larger target. Verbatim points:
- If this gets really good, it REPLACES the actual battle map.
- Use the elevation map 'to create a more realistic LOS system than Foundry would normally support' for mechs.
- Density target: 'perhaps literally x100 more complex and dense than the current version... a map like Cities Skylines where we draw a line for every road, every alley, every ramshackle shop, every temple, every carpark, every motorway, trainline, tram system, every skyscraper and every roadside shrine. I'm talking insane levels of complexity.'
- 'The terrain needs to be fine and grainy for that to work too, though the contours could be realistically set to real world expectations of accuracy.'
- Mechs are produced from a SEA FORT off the coast; build a system for placing forts offshore, 'better yet we'll eventually let the players use this same system to plan to change the map.'
- BIOMES generated from the map; certain mechs work better in certain biomes; dense urban areas provide cover automatically 'because it's so easy to hide between buildings'.
- Persistent scarring: 'any combat in an area can leave scars and shots which miss eventually land somewhere in the city.'
- CRITICAL CONSTRAINT, and the one that unlocks the rest: 'The map only updates between sessions, not mid session, so you will always be able to take your time to make it work.' Generation is an offline batch job. Minutes or an hour are fine. Only LOS queries and Foundry scene loading have to be fast.

Full architecture is now in design/map-generation.md, written 2026-08-23 and backed by benchmarks run the same day. Headline measured results: erosion is O(n^2.6) so 2048^2 (6.25 m) is ~20 min and 12800^2 (1 m) is not viable; a 1 m Int16 raster over 12.8 km is 0.31 GB (Float64 would be 1.22 GB); an LOS ray costs ~4 us, i.e. ~250k rays/sec, making a full 360-degree viewshed about 4 ms. Three architectural conclusions follow: physics stays coarse and detail arrives by AMPLIFICATION not simulation; elevation LOS is cheap enough to run speculatively; and fine detail (alleys, buildings) must be VECTOR rather than raster, since a 2-3 m alley cannot exist on a 2 m grid but is exact and nearly free as a polyline.

Two design revisions this forces on the stage-1 write-up above:
(1) The 'damage event log' is too narrow. If players can PLAN map changes, construction and destruction are the same mechanism — an ordered, append-only OPERATION log (crater / collapse / construct / reclaim / dredge / override). Unapplied operations are then speculative branches, which is exactly what a player plan is.
(2) The city does not sit ON the terrain, it RESHAPES it. Road cut-and-fill, benched building platforms, railway cuttings, sea walls, dredged channels, reclaimed land — in a real Japanese port city a huge fraction of near-surface terrain is anthropogenic. Terrain must be WRITABLE by the city stage, which stage 1 does not allow.

A mechanical consequence worth recording because it justifies the whole LOS effort: a Frame is 'building-sized' (~15 m, four or five storeys) and a 1950s Japanese town is 2-3 storey timber at 6-10 m, so THE TOWN COMES UP TO A FRAME'S CHEST. A Frame sees over the old quarter's fabric but not over ridges, the gasworks, or the few concrete modern buildings; a kid at 1.6 m sees only the street they are in. Two scales get genuinely different pictures of the world from one dataset.
sourceContext: Ingram raised it as a self-described 'side quest' after finding the existing AI-generated satellite battle map too ugly to keep using. Full approach designed in the same conversation and approved for stage-1 implementation immediately.
openSubQuestions: Does the city get a name, and is that Ingram's creative call to make now or a tracked naming-placeholder for later? See data/campaign/naming-placeholders.json.

Which of the reference art's specific landmarks are hard constraints the generator must be steered to produce (the sea-fort in the channel, the causeway, the aqueducts, the smokestack waterfront) vs. things hand-placed onto generated terrain afterward?

Is Layer D (patch-synthesis amplification from real Japanese DEM) wanted at all — and if so, is sourcing real GSI/GEBCO data into the repo acceptable, given reference/ and the Foundry trees are already gitignored bulk third-party material?
How far does the campaign-long damage log actually need to go — updated per session, or only at arc beats?

What is the actual density target, as a number? '100x' is not falsifiable. design/map-generation.md proposes ~80,000 buildings and ~500 km of road centreline over 12.8 km, estimated from real Japanese urban densities — needs confirming or replacing before stages 5-7.
Does the city have a real-world analogue Ingram wants it to resemble (Onomichi, Kobe, Atami, Hakodate, Sasebo...)? Would settle a great many art-direction parameters at once.
Sea forts: hand-designed template instantiated procedurally, or fully generated? And is the reference-art sea-fort-plus-causeway a fixed landmark the generator must be steered to accommodate?
Do players' map-change plans need to RENDER speculatively (a proposed operation log rendered but not committed), or is it enough to describe them and apply between sessions?

Rill density from stage 2 is uniform across every hillside, where real terrain varies it by aspect, lithology and vegetation. Cosmetic and only visible at close zoom - worth a pass when the map is being looked at closely, or leave it?
resolution:
STAGES 1-2 SHIPPED 2026-08-23 (tools/map-generator/). Architecture, measured limits and the revised 9-stage plan are in design/map-generation.md. Stages 3-9 not started.

STAGE 2 (amplification, tools/map-generator/terrain/amplify.mjs + descriptors.mjs): coarse physics grid -> fine detail grid. Measured end to end: 512^2 physics at 25 m in 27 s, amplified x8 to 4096^2 at 3.13 m in a further 22 s, 857 MB peak, 32 MB Int16 DTM, 1,360 km of 1 m contour line in the first 20 m of relief. Structure preservation 0.016 m mean / 0.34 m max.

Three findings that changed the design, all measured rather than assumed:
(1) EXEMPLAR SYNTHESIS TURNED OUT UNNECESSARY. Ingram's half-remembered patch-based paper was expected to be the mechanism here. It is not needed: isotropic noise smeared along local flow lines by line integral convolution reads as downhill rills, and is self-consistent with the drainage network in a way borrowed texture could not be. An earlier attempt that rotated the noise sample FRAME per pixel failed visibly - the rotation angle varies across space so the pattern tears, ruling straight seams across the terrain.
(2) AMPLIFICATION ONLY WORKS AT A LARGE FACTOR. The restore pass deletes anything whose block average is non-zero, so synthesised detail has to sit between the fine grid's Nyquist limit and about half a coarse block. At factor 4 that band is empty and amplification measurably does nothing. Factor 8+ required.
(3) THE PLANNED FINE-SCALE EROSION REFINEMENT IS COUNTERPRODUCTIVE, and now defaults off. Measured roughness gain 2.24x with it OFF, 1.86x at intended settings, 1.51x with the timestep cranked 50x. It runs with no uplift against a fixed base level, so it has no driving force at all - erosion under those conditions can only relax a surface toward grade, never create relief, so it smoothed away the detail it was meant to sharpen. Making it work needs a base-level fall or continued uplift; the code is kept behind refineIterations.

Also done: computeStack replaced with Braun & Willett's O(n) donor-list traversal (1.4-1.7x faster, 1024^2+ now reachable). That corrected an earlier claim in the design doc - the elevation sort was a constant factor, not the asymptotic problem; both versions scale ~O(cells^1.06) and MEMORY, not time, is the real wall.

104 tests in test/map-generator/, all passing.

tools/map-generator/ (see its README). Erosion + transgression -> coastline, bathymetry, rivers, contours, harbour sites and river mouths, rendered as a self-contained SVG with an embedded shaded-relief raster. 77 tests in test/map-generator/, all passing, 380/380 project-wide.

Built as designed, with two things that only emerged from making it actually work:

(1) A SECOND EROSION PHASE. 'Erode then flood' has a flaw the design did not anticipate: phase 1 builds its coastal plain at the glacial lowstand, and the transgression then drowns exactly that plain, leaving mountains dropping into deep water and nowhere flat for a town. Correct physics, useless map. The fix is the real history — post-transgression (Holocene) alluviation, run against the NEW shoreline as base level, with deposition made transport-limited (scaled by Scrit/(S+Scrit)) so alluvium fills valley floors instead of blanketing hillsides. Measured: flat lowland +37%, and it also trims the over-fractal 170 km phase-1 coastline to a plausible 45-64 km. This is what produces the harbour and the town site as two parts of one landform.

(2) An exact Euclidean distance transform (Felzenszwalb & Huttenlocher) replaced a chamfer approximation, whose directional ridges were being contoured by the shelf-break bathymetry into straight-edged polygonal terraces in deep water. Matters beyond that artefact because distance-to-water is a field the city stage will zone off.

Tuned defaults (512 cells at 25 m = 12.8 km): ~980 m relief, 45 km of coastline in 6 rings, 24 harbour sites, ~45 s to generate. Parameters are physical and the tuning target is the stream power law's equilibrium slope (~37% hillslope, ~2% channel at 1 km2) — see DEFAULT_PARAMS.

Also answers world-map-satellite-combat's open sub-question about how satellite-scale and battle-scale scenes relate: ONE vector model rendered at two scales. At FEET_PER_SQUARE=50 a grid square is ~15 m, larger than a house, so individual buildings are not representable on the tactical grid at all. The city view's unit is the block; the battle view crops a neighbourhood and its unit is the building. Vector-first is what makes that dual render possible, and is a further reason not to generate a raster.

STAGES 2-4 NOT STARTED: tensor-field streets, blocks/parcels/buildings and naming, the damage event log, and the Foundry raster-and-walls bake.

REAL-DATA PIVOT (2026-08-24, superseding the plan above for terrain/city generation specifically -- see design/map-generation.md, rewritten 2026-08-23/24). The fully-procedural terrain+city pipeline above is no longer the plan for the CAMPAIGN MAP: the city is now real OSM + GSI DEM data (real Kobe, rotated, renamed, fictionalised), not generated from a seed. tools/map-generator/ (this entry's subject) keeps a real, narrower role per that doc's §9 -- amplification and offshore bathymetry, both still directly useful -- and is not superseded as a tool, only as THE plan for where the city comes from. The operation-log design this entry originated (§6 above) survived the pivot essentially unchanged and is now being implemented in tools/city-map/ (Python, not this tool's Node/JS) against the real data.

MILESTONE 0 SHIPPED 2026-08-24 (tools/city-map/): the real-data render pipeline rescued out of a session scratchpad into a tested, modular Python package -- parsing, multipolygon relation reconstruction, sea/land classification, hillshade, contours, and tiled rendering, all working end-to-end against real Kobe/Kurose data and verified visually against the previously-approved render. 231 tests in test/city-map/.

Rescuing it surfaced three real bugs that had shipped in the approved render, each fixed with a regression test (see tools/city-map/citymap/*.py module docstrings for the full diagnosis of each): (1) an Overpass relation query with no size sanity check reconstructing Honshu itself (228,438 km2) and silently costing every render 30-40s of wasted geometry work; (2) a terrain-vs-building shadow direction mismatch, proven via first-principles derivation of PIL's rotation convention plus an empirical marker test, not by inspection; (3) a NaN-elevation fill strategy for hillshade that used the frame-wide mean (mountain-inflated, measured 113.9 m against a real range of -11 to 715 m) rather than sea level, which manufactured a fake elevated plateau across the entire open sea and produced phantom shadow patches on real coastal features -- confirmed directly: Port Island read fully-shadowed under the old fill and correctly unshadowed once fixed to fill at sea level.

Not yet built: the operation log itself, the road router (state-lattice design specified, not implemented), parametric templates, and the page-furniture render pass (paper texture, labels, cartouche, compass rose -- ported reference only, in tools/city-map/_spike8_reference.py).

MILESTONE 1 SHIPPED 2026-08-23 (tools/city-map/citymap/ops/): the vertical slice -- operation log, road router, parametric templates, and terrain editing -- built, tested, and run end to end against real data via a real CLI (tools/city-map/render.py). demolish.py removes content cleanly with graph-cascade road pruning (a bridge to a removed island is eaten back to the real junction it branches from, never left as a stub) and two mutually-exclusive outcomes for what the cleared ground becomes: leaveLanduse (stays dry land, tinted) or returnToSea (the actual inverse of land reclamation -- unions the area into World.sea, so it renders as open water with a fresh coastline). construct.py places a parametric template, routes its access road with a curvature-hard-constrained state-lattice A* (router.py -- proven, not just asserted, why a plain cost-surface router cannot produce real switchbacks), and benches a level platform into the slope (builds terrain UP to the site's highest sampled point, not down to the lowest -- documented reasoning: cutting to the low corner leaves the frontage at unchanged natural grade with no vantage, building up to the high corner puts the whole pad above the naturally lower ground beyond it).

The demo op log (data/map/operations/kurose.json) removes Kobe Airport via returnToSea and constructs an 8-part mech-bunker template (angular chamfered hangar, blast-deflector wings, rear revetment, a separated generator shed, a guard post, a fan-shaped apron, and a looped perimeter patrol track as a genuine line-typed part, not another filled polygon) in the mountains northwest of downtown.

Two real placement bugs were found by the USER looking at renders, not by the test suite, and both are now load-bearing checks rather than one-off fixes: (1) an early bunker site sat 12m from a live railway -- construct.py had NO check against non-building infrastructure at all until this forced one (ConstructReport.footprintClear/footprintConflicts); (2) after that fix, an auto-picked clear site turned out to straddle a real stream -- the conflict check didn't cover water yet either, and now does (buildings, highways, railways, waterways and water-body polygons, matching render.py's own water-detection logic exactly so construct can never disagree with what actually renders blue). The terrain-benching feature itself was ALSO user-requested mid-session, specifically to stop future sites needing to be hunted for naturally-flat ground at all.

Also built this milestone: TemplatePart 'line' kind (a template can include real linear features -- tracks, fences -- not just filled area polygons); World.TerrainEdit as a new frame-invariant record type (the actual raster edit happens once per frame in fields.apply_terrain_edits, keeping World itself rotation/extent-independent like everything else in it); a dependency-free progress bar + stage timer (citymap/progress.py) and a real CLI (render.py, not a throwaway script) with preview/overview/full modes, so a person can run and babysit a full-resolution export themselves; and a genuine data bug caught mid-session -- the on-disk World cache predated a Feature.to_attrs fix and silently carried zero osm_way_id values, which would have made demolish.py's graph-cascade pruning a no-op against real data despite passing all its synthetic tests; fixed by bumping world.PARSER_VERSION so a stale cache can never silently pass as current again.

Not yet built: offshore construction (sea forts -- reclaiming land in open water and causeway routing instead of road routing; planned in ideas/entries/offshore-construction.json, not a surprise gap but deliberately scoped out of this milestone since it touches three separate pieces of new machinery), the grammar module (§5 -- road classes/grades use fixed defaults, not the imported city's own measured statistics), and the page-furniture render pass.
resolvedSubQuestions: Is the generated map REPLACING tools/battle-simulator/assets/battle-map.jpg outright? — ANSWERED 2026-08-23: YES, conditional on quality ('if we make this really really good then yes we'd replace the actual battle map'). The downstream cost stands and must be paid in the same change: the simulator's deployment positions reference features of the jpg by description ('the darker structure at the map's bottom-left', the foothills at the far side), so those scenarios and their tests need updating when the swap happens.
